utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. If I could remind you, sir, of the affirmation you took at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, if we could go into private session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to those claims, have you ever been confronted by anyone from the Prosecution with a statement of his, of (redacted)'s, claiming and stating that you are lying about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The information that you received from a member of your family, without identifying who the individual was, with regard to Murrizi was that Murrizi was a gentleman named Agim Murtezi. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct. The information for Murrizi was that his name was Agim Murtezi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on the information that you received, you then told others that Murrizi was Agim Murtezi, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I received information, I didn't see Agim Murtezi, I didn't see him at the moment I had his photo. I saw him in the prison, at the cherry tree, and at the execution site --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, that's not the question that I asked you. The question that I asked you was a simple one which was: "Based on the information that you received, you told others that Murrizi was Agim Murtezi, didn't you?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't mean -- what you mean "others"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Others, for example, investigators from the CCIU.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The information that you received regarding Agim Murtezi was wrong, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the information turned out to be wrong, when they showed me the photo line-up I couldn't tell who Murrizi was or Agim Murtezi, as they say, to sign his name and his number. If I weren't sure about him like I was about Shala, Qerqizi, Celiku, I couldn't do anything about Murtezi, I couldn't write his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again, the information that you received - that is what I'm focusing on - is that the information that you received was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm objecting to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: May I finish my question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'm objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm objecting on two grounds. The first ground is that the question has been asked and answered. The second is that it's not really for this witness to say whether the information is wrong or not. He has given his evidence in this issue and it's not for him to say whether it's wrong or not. But in any case, the question has been put to him and he answered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I disagree with Mr. Whiting's analysis on two issues. First of all, with regard to the information this witness has received, he has the ability to render an opinion as to whether or not it was correct or incorrect information in the same fashion that he has rendered an opinion with regard to other information he as received as being correct or incorrect. And it's obviously for the Trial Chamber to make an ultimate determination in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That was the first proposition. Were there two?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, there are. The second is that I don't believe that he's answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think he's made in this atmosphere a normal attempt at answering, but I'm not going to stop your exploring on the basis of opinion, where complicated by the problem of hearsay and searching into the quality of the substance of information given as something which I think can be useful to the Chamber. So halfway each on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were attempting, as were other individuals who are (redacted) - and once again without mentioning anybody in that regard by any further identification - to find out who were the people responsible at various times for various activities that you experienced. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you please ask the question again. I'm not clear about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. I'm more than happy to. You wanted to find out, for example, at one point in time who were the individuals who took you from your home; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also seeked [sic] to get the names of the individuals who you were about and around or who were around you in Lapusnik. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you at the time that you were attempting to get this information --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I suppose we should go into private session for but a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to the third soldier who was at the execution site, do you recall ever giving anybody any information concerning his physical characteristics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember having an information about him. And as for him, as I mentioned it in the statement, he was just opposite to me and he was shooting at my direction. I don't know whether he's alive now or whether he's dead. I don't know where he is. I don't know him at all. But I always thought that although he was given an order to shoot me, maybe he had a soul, maybe that's why he didn't kill me, maybe that's why I managed to escape. I don't remember giving his description to anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you were trying to do throughout this process of identification, your attempting to identify who these people were, was you were attempting to collect all the information you possibly could about them so you would know who they were. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Out of these persons, number one for us to find was Shala. Every movement in regard to (redacted) was to find out who Shala is, who this man is, where he comes from, where his house is. And this was achieved. The person was found, his identity was found, who his father was was found. So this person is sitting just behind you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had information concerning where the third soldier came from, and by that I mean you had information that the third soldier, according Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to you, came from somebody named Celiku. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean. Did he come from a place called Celiku or what do you mean by Celiku?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. That he was sent by an individual named Celiku to help, as you put it, Shala. That was information you had; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is how it was. On our way uphill from the prison, this soldier was not with us; and on halfway, he was assigned to us. We met with these people, and it's there where Shala said that Commander Celiku is coming. And this is when this soldier joined us. And up to that point, we didn't have any soldier with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, with regard to this particular piece of information, the piece of information concerning Celiku, this is a pretty important information. And you didn't share this information with anybody. You didn't give this information to anybody, the Serbs or CCIU, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection. That misstates the evidence. He did give it to CCIU.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not initially, not at the outset.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that's what I'm getting at. At the outset when you're looking for these people, not when you've gone step by step and worked through a plan with the investigator what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was there a CCIU initially?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No. The initial statements were made to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's -- your attempt to respond I think added another confusion to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm actually not trying to confuse evidence, although it's often something that Defence attorneys are accused of trying to do. I'm trying to actually clarify things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first met with the Serb authorities, you didn't mention the name of Celiku, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't mention this name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Topolski. Cross-examined by Mr. Topolski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I represent Isak Musliu. I want to understand your position. You are committed to seeking justice, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The search for justice for you takes the legal route, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have abandoned the Kanun, you have abandoned blood revenge. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by abandoning the Kanun and blood (redacted). What are you referring to? I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to what you told ICTY investigators, that you and your family discussed whether you should murder those responsible for the death of (redacted). You abandoned that and chose the legal route, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was discussion amongst family members how to proceed from the moment of the killing. And we opted for the legal way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from now on, sir, we can take out of account, can we, any idea that you are sitting here to get revenge? That's not the case. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not -- I don't understand you clearly. What revenge are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on. I want to ask you some questions, not many, about Murrizi. And I'm not going to repeat the questions you've been asked already. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The research that you and others were able to carry out gave Murrizi the name Agim Murtezi, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how it was. That's how we found that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A man called Agim Murtezi appeared in a dock very much like the one behind me in about February 2003. Did you see that on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very well. I saw it very well, and I saw that a person came here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you pick up a telephone and tell anyone they got the wrong man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why shall I pick up the phone?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you want justice; you don't want revenge. That's why. You knew the man Agim Murtezi in this dock behind me was not Murrizi. What did you do about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before Agim Murtezi got to this bench of the accused, CCIU showed me six pictures. The first set was of Shala and then of Qerqiz and then of Celiku. They didn't say whether you know someone from Lapusnik or whether you know someone from there or here. I looked carefully at the pictures, and then when I was shown Agim Murtezi's pictures I wasn't sure who that person was. So that's why I couldn't circle his number and sign. And when the ICTY brought him here, I don't have the power to change -- to make changes to that. As for other witnesses, whether there was a mistake or something, this matter is not in my hands. I saw him here. I was just watching and waiting what will happen. But as for me, it was difficult to circle his name and sign it because I didn't know this person. That's why. Why should I pick up the phone? Who shall I call?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not responsible for sending him here; he comes here, he could have stood trial and been convicted for all you know or for all you care. Is that your position regarding Agim Murtezi, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As to whether he could have been sentenced based on other witness statements, I have nothing to do with it. But as for me, I can say that I could not identify him on that picture. I couldn't say personally that this person is Agim Murtezi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have to repeat your answers for us all to understand them. Would you like to send an apology to him now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you like to apologise to Agim Murtezi for misnaming him as a man who shot at you and others? Can you give him an apology now? Now's your chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I hear the objection. I don't accept the objection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, answer my question. Do you want to apologise or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have apologised to him if I said that this person is Agim Murtezi. On that case, I would apologise. But I looked at those pictures very carefully and I cannot say that this person was in Lapusnik. So I don't see the need for me to apologise to him. Tell me, why should I apologise? Give me the reason, and then I will apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't answer your questions; you answer mine. And I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But this is my answer. I don't see a need to apologise because I did not identify that person on the pictures that were shown as a person who was at the killing. It is very difficult to circle someone's name when you're not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You give names when you're not sure, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I heard that Murrizi was a person called Agim Murtezi, but when the investigators showed me the pictures and asked me to identify who was Agim Murtezi from those pictures, I couldn't identify him. So I had the pictures before me. There were six on that line-up. And I was supposed to identify the person, but I couldn't pick up the pen and circle the number because I didn't know who the person was. And then the photo line-up was taken from me, I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can we go into private session just for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to see if I can establish with you as closely I can the dates between which you were held at Lapusnik according to you. Let's work together. First of all, can you give us a date in July 1998 when you say you were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I know it was two weeks after Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the kidnapping of (redacted). I think it was two weeks after; I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that event that you've just referred to occurred about the 4th of July, let's see if we can't get to a date together. On the 18th of July you were with SUP, weren't you, talking about to Serb police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know on which date I was in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you it was the 18th. We have a document, and you and I together are going to be looking at it in a little while. So it's not the 18th. How many days after your interview with SUP in [sic] (redacted) and (redacted) to be exact, how many days after that interview with (redacted) and (redacted) were you taken, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. After this day a meeting was held in the school building. I don't know exactly when that meeting was held, but I know that it was on that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to try and help you. It looks from other evidence that that was probably the 20th of July. Now, we know that Lapusnik fell to the Serbs on the 26th of July. We also know that the terrible events in the forest occurred on that day or probably the day before, the 25th of July; which would mean, if I'm right, sir, that you spent perhaps five days and nights in the place you have described as the camp. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the first three nights, I spent them with (redacted), with (redacted), with (redacted). Musli Belince was there as well and a person from Varigovc village. I spent the first three days with the above-mentioned persons. On the last day Isak blindfolded me, and I mentioned it in my statement what he did to me. So he blindfolded me and took me to the other room. And to my recollection, I spent four days there in the second room. Maybe it's three, but as far as I remember it was four. I don't know dates, but I know this in days. I know that I spent three nights in the first room. I know that I've been there three nights and three days and that (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is clear from your evidence is that the beatings that you say you received from Qerqiz you received during those first three days. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, the reasons I ask you these questions, sir, are these: That it is my client's case, and therefore I put it to you for your comment, that between lunchtime on the 18th of July and midday on the 24th of July, he was not in Lapusnik, he was fighting in Rahovec. Now, if I'm right about that, he wasn't there when you were there. Would you care to comment about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You think that Isak was in Rahovec fighting; this is your opinion. But my opinion is that I never ever believed that Isak was fighting in Rahovec. Why? Because on that day when he entered the room with Murrizi and with the soldiers and ordered them to chain me up and when he started to punch me and hit me and when he jumped and hit me on the chest and then I fell on the ground and he started kicking me, this Isak here beating us there and with a soldier behind holding us at gunpoint, this Isak was not fighting there. I am convinced that he never ever went out to fight. What he could do was to find someone, to tie him up, to beat him. This is what I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You used the words "believe" and "convince" I lot, Witness. Have you become convinced that it was Isak Musliu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where? On a fighting or beating me? Where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you become convinced it was Isak Musliu beating you? Is that what you believe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Without thinking, I have seen him there. A person whom I knew from before the war who I've seen before the war. What do you mean by believe?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come back to that. Have you ever been an informant for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never. Whatever I say here you will take it a different way, but I was never an informant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have any of your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't even interested to become one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll talk about interests later. Have any of (redacted) been informants for the Serbs, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you after 1990 require a permit to keep a gun in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave (redacted) permission to keep a gun after 1990 in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will tell you this: (redacted) was a hunter. He had weapons in his possession in 1980s while Tito was still alive. After 1972, when Kosovo gained its autonomy and when the Albanians were ruling, the head of the SUP in Ferizaj and in Shtime was Albanian. So (redacted) got another hunting rifle. This was a hobby for my family. (redacted), God bless his soul, he would often stop his work and go to hunt. This was a hobby throughout this time. It's not a hobby that we bought from some -- this is something we loved and love knows of no boundaries. I, too, went on hunting. There were rumours that I was going out to hunt without permission for my weapon, that I was using (redacted) weapon without any permission. At that time I had the opportunity to get a permission to use (redacted) weapon. At that time it was the same thing, like to get a permission, a driving licence. It was even more difficult to get a passport or a driving licence than a hunting permission. The Government of Kosovo was functioning at that time, although they were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness go slower, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please pause a moment. The interpreters can't keep up with you. You're pouring out a great deal of information very quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will comply with the requests. We replied to every appeal that we received from the Government of Kosovo. At that time you had to pay a tax to the Kosovo government, not only us but the -- everybody, the entire population of Kosovo. Whatever we had to do on a national level, whatever was in the interests of the people of Kosova, we did. We boycotted the elections --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, we're about 25.000 miles away from the question that I asked you, which is: What gave (redacted) permission to have a gun in 1990. And I think the answer is an Albanian who was head of SUP in Ferizaj at the time. Now, you'll leave that witness box, you know,if you stop making speeches and listen to the questions and answer them. Now, I want to ask you this: You deny being a Serb informant. You deny any member of (redacted) was a Serb informant. Was it ever suggested to you to your knowledge by anyone in Kosovo before the war that you were a Serb informant? Have you ever been accused of being such a thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In the light of those answers, I'd like to have in Albanian in front of you the text of your interview with the Serbs of the 18th of July, 1998. Mr. Mansfield had this yesterday. It's in his bundle I think. And it's the third document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I hope the Court still has Mr. Mansfield's bundle from yesterday. It's got a frontispiece on it like that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Do you have an ERN number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Sure. In English U000-0691 to 0692 in what I believe to be Albanian 0691 -- oh, the same number, to 0692, but it's immediately following the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked questions about this yesterday or at least parts of it by Mr. Mansfield on behalf of Mr. Limaj. And I appreciate we're going to have to be careful because there are names in this document. But before we start looking at it in your language and in mine, there's something else I want to ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to ask a question or make an appeal. If we could go into private session for this because it -- I would be able to explain things better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Of course we will, but before we go into private session, I want to ask you something publicly and it's this: You made a number of statements to ICTY investigators, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope you'll take it from me, but of course you can have it in front of you if you wish to. I am looking at the statement you made on the 8th and 9th of October of 2003. I'm not looking at that document you've got there for a moment, so you can put that down. I'd like you to listen. This is what you said to the ICTY in a statement on that date: "I have never referred to the KLA as terrorists and would never think of the KLA as such. They were our army and were fighting legitimately for Kosovo. Despite all I have witnessed and all I have been through, I do not blame the KLA generally for what happened. In my opinion, it is a few people who were members of our army that are responsible, and it is they are to blame and not the KLA as a whole."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Younis has ever, very kindly, has handed over a copy of that statement in Albanian I imagine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you go to paragraph 15 of it, you'll see that I've just read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which number -- which is number 15?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1-5, on the fourth page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Good. I just want to ask you, sir, to confirm to Their Honours, please, that this is both true and accurate a statement of your position, namely that you have never referred to the KLA as terrorists, would never think of them as such, and they were to you "our army." Is that what you believed then and is that what you believe today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will answer, and I will answer slowly so that you will -- you will understand. All -- the three people in the dock there are from Kosovo, but as far as I can see nobody else is here from Yugoslavia. At that time when you went to the SUP, even if they asked me at the SUP if the KLA were terrorists, I would say yes. Because there was no other way to get out of that door, of Jasovic's door, if I had not answered like that. These people have done those things, but the people of Kosovo, the KLA, have fought for freedom against the Serbian regime. The same thing was said here by Dr. Rugova in Milosevic's case. The same thing he said when he went to Belgrade. He admitted things --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interrupting because you have to slow down. Wait, please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have to slow down and perhaps you have to stop making speeches. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will try to speak slowly. I will try to clarify this. What things were like then in Pristina. Because this person was sent to Belgrade by force to -- Rugova was sent to Belgrade by force to shake hands with Milosevic because he was forced to do so. And you're mentioning this statement. Even if he had asked me if my mother was a member of the KLA I would have said yes because otherwise I would not have seen the light of day. In addition to that, fighting has started there in areas of Kosovo. The KLA fought for the freedom of Kosovo, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know what's coming, don't you? You know the questions I'm going to ask you about this statement, don't you? Answer me, please. Do you know what's coming? Do you know what I'm about to ask you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the things I'm about to ask you is why this statement is full of the word "terrorists." Of course this is a statement made to someone who's never been to your house for a drink. (redacted) never came to your house for a friendly drink, did he?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I apologise for the interruption. I just note when counsel put this statement to the witness he asked if we could go into private session and counsel indicated he would -- well, I just wanted to remind everyone that that had been said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, I'm very grateful for the reminder. I hope I'm imposing enough self discipline. These matters, in my respectful submission, are properly and appropriately canvassed in open court -- open session. When the time comes to consider the text, it was my intention and still is, that that is the time to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the proper course to try to follow, unless the witness gets into difficulties with the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course. It is not my intention nor object to create that situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this statement that we're about to look at is full of the word "terrorists," and I was just asking you that it's a statement made to a man who has made a statement to this Tribunal in which he has said (redacted) that he comes to your house for drunks. Now, were you surprised to hear him say that in a statement to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour -- excuse me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it. I don't see it. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt again, but that's not what it says in the statement. He does not -- there's a present tense/past tense problem in the way the question has been posed. And I hate to be picky but it's important. That is, there is no statement that he comes to his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to read from Mr. (redacted)'s statement signed by this -- signed to this Tribunal that is dated the 11th of May. Witness, I hope you're following me. It's paragraph 14. "On the 1st of August somebody came from a place to a police station, 1st of August, 1998," you -- I'm not reading from that statement. Has he been given it? Is that (redacted) statement? Oh, well, thank you. I'm grateful. It's not (redacted) statement. Put that down, please, Witness, if you wouldn't mind. That's not what I'm reading you. I'm reading from the statement of (redacted) that says: "On the 1st of August 1998," you "from" your village "came to a police station to report that you'd been held in a prison. I remember this date because I knew," and he gives your first name only, "and his (redacted) were friendly people who didn't oppose the Serb authorities. I often stopped," past tense, "by their house for a drink and I went hunting with them." Are you surprised to hear that Mr. (redacted) from MUP [sic] says that about you and (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not surprised. But you have the wrong person because there -- the family (redacted) had many members. There was another one who was a hunter who went with (redacted) hunting. I'm not denying here that (redacted) had Serbian friends. From Tito's time to then going on to the time of the autonomy and later on. But he went on hunting with Serbs and not with Serbs. But this person from the police here, he is not the one who went hunting; he is another one. His name is -- he worked at Ljuboten hotel. He was the one that came to our home. We drank coffee and we went hunting. But this is different. It's another person, not the one that you have there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you need a break? Are you getting tired? I want you to do justice to your answers. Do you need a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have the statement here in front of me of (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: tells the Tribunal in the third paragraph of his statement that in April 1991 he joined SUP in Urosevac. His father was a police officer. This isn't another (redacted), it's the same Serb policeman who drank at your house. Now, do you want to change the answer you've just given us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean (redacted) was an officer? I didn't understand that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted) The only thing that he had was his guns, his hunting guns, from Tito's time, from the time of the autonomy to the time of Slobodan Milosevic, and I cannot deny that. When we speak about the time that I went to the SUP office, well, I had to answer what he wanted me to answer about the KLA or everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- I'm going to interrupt because I'm going to ask you about that. More importantly Mr. Whiting is on his feet, so I give way to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish I had raised this earlier, but it took me a moment to find the statement Mr. Topolski is referring to. I think out of fairness the rest of the paragraph that Mr. Topolski was reading from should be read, since the insinuation at bottom is -- that has been put to this witness was that he was providing information. And if I could just read the remainder of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: To make it clear, I certainly was intending to put it. I wanted to get some answers first and then I was going to come back to it. But I'm happy for Mr. Whiting to read it out if he wishes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The remainder of this paragraph is in reference to this witness and his family: "I would not say they were loyal Albanians in the negative way and we never used them for getting intelligence information. They were just people who didn't make a difference between different ethnicities. Anyway, this could have been enough reason for the Albanian separatists to have the desire to kidnap them."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you loyal Albanians, you and (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the national issue, yes. Of course, without any doubt. When the issue was about national -- our national identity. But to get a birth certificate or to get a licence, we had to go to the Serbs for those, to the municipality, to the police. We had to get our IDs. The everyday things that were important to us, we had to go to them, not only me but also the number one in Kosovo, Dr. Ibrahim Rugova, he had to do that as well. But it's another issue if you ask, Have you ever worked for the police? There were people at the time who were Albanians and who worked at the municipality, were heads of the municipality, mayors or so on. But for us we never had anything to do with the regime except, you know, the hobby, the hunting. I said hunting and love are the same -- are very similar. They don't know boundaries, colour. When you love something, you love something. You love basketball, you love football. These are things -- This is how we went together hunting with some Serbs; this is what happened and I don't deny it. And we still do it today. There are no Serbs anymore, but (redacted) still goes hunting with Albanian friends. At that time there were Albanians as well who went hunting, but we had Serbs as well with us. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it might be an appropriate moment. I wonder if when in retirement the Court might consider some gentle words to the witness regarding the apparent advisability as some might think of simply answering the questions as asked. Obviously one recognises the other aspect of this Court's function on the world stage, but, Your Honour, there comes a time when the Court's time may not be being most efficaciously spent. And I wonder if the Court might consider saying something to the witness on its return. I hate to interrupt a witness and say, Now answer my question; it sounds so lame. Your Honour, may I leave that thought with the Court during its adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Court to date has been conscious that the witness is in the hands of experienced counsel and that their attempts have not proved very useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I don't know that any intervention from the Chamber will. We will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour might want to consider trying it once and see how we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We need a further 30-minute break because of the redactions. We will resume at a quarter past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Topolski is now to ask you some more questions. Could I just ask you to try and keep in mind two things. First, if you could answer more slowly, the interpreters will have a chance to keep up with you. We are interpreting into four different languages and it becomes very hard when you speak very quickly. The second thing I want to suggest to you is that you try and keep clearly in your mind the question that's asked by counsel. You seem to have a tendency to start off to answer that question, but then you drift away and start to tell a long story related to the question or where -- about what you think the question is leading to. All you need to do is listen to the question and if you know the answer, give the answer. And you've no need to go on to explain anything about the answer. Just give the answer as shortly as you can and try to do it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. reasonably slowly, if you could. And I think that might help everyone to get through the matter more quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm very much obliged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told the Court on a large number of occasions that neither you nor any (redacted) cooperated with the Serb authorities. I want to ask you a very specific question on that subject, please. And in fairness to you, I'm going to indicate to you what is sitting here on my desk in front of me. Just handed to me are the minutes of a meeting dated the 20th of May, 1992. It is a meeting of the Presidency of the LDK branch for the area in which your village was situated. First of all, do you understand me so far?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me, could we be provided with a copy of whatever it is you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. It's in Albanian, but you're very welcome to. I've had it translated for me in the last half-hour. It's a rather rough-and-ready translation that we had provided literally in the last half-hour. I'm very happy to provide him with a copy, if that will help him. Can I take Mr. Guy-Smith's. I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could it also be provided to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No, because I'm just going to put the conclusion of the meeting to him and ask him if he became aware of the conclusion. The contents of the meeting are not for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This meeting resolved that you and (redacted) should be boycotted because you continued to cooperate with the Serb police. First question I ask you: Do you understand what the word "boycott" means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand it very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only question that I can properly ask you arising from this meeting seems to me to be this: Did you become aware of a boycott of (redacted) in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to know what boycott this is about. Is it for -- boycotted for weddings, for deaths, for funerals? What does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Everything. People were not to speak to you, to have anything to do with you, to go to your house, to boycott you. I want to know whether you became aware of such a decision by this branch of the LDK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't -- I'm going to object and I don't know if this rough translation is before the Court, but there's -- there are two points -- and maybe I'm just missing it because it's just handed to me at this last moment and not beforehand, but number one, it talks about noncooperation with the police and not cooperation with the police. And secondly, there's no reference to this witness in here, as was put to him in the question by Mr. Topolski: "This meeting resolved that you and (redacted) should be boycotted because you continued to cooperate with the Serb police." I don't see any mention of his name in here, the witness, nor do I see any mention of cooperation. It's talking about noncooperation. I'm a little -- just a little perplexed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, let me see if I can help Mr. Whiting's perplexities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The effect of this decision, as I understand it, of this branch of this political party was that it was believed that members of (redacted) (redacted) were cooperating with the Serb police and a decision was made ordered by the LDK that people should have nothing to do with (redacted) (redacted). Now, the only question I can ask you is: Were you aware of such a thing in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The objection, Mr. Topolski, is that there is no adequate foundation in the document for the premise upon which the question is put. We don't have the document, of course, but do you say that there is an expressed mention of the witness and (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: There is not an expressed mention of the witness; there is mention of the witness's (redacted) by name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Simply the surname of the (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we are in open session now and I am going to be careful, very careful I hope, about names and I know you will be as well. We are looking together at the contents of a statement signed by you. It is said on or about the (redacted), when you were interviewed by (redacted) and (redacted). I was asking you whether you were saying many of the things written here, and up to now you have said that effectively you had no choice but that you were simply repeating things they wanted you to say. I want to go on in the document. "On many occasions," it says, "in the late evening hours a dark-coloured Jeep was seen in a village where the terrorists were staying. I heard that the so-called KLA members from villages," and they're listed, including places like Suva Reka, "were also staying in a someone's house," and you name that person, in a village called Laniste. My question is this: Did you tell the Serbs this or is this again you simply putting down what they told you to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the same thing as it is now with you. You are reading a statement and that's what they did. They would ask, Is this person a member? Yes. At that time, I will repeat it again, there were members from my village, members of the KLA. And the persons who were interrogating me, they did not know this. I can verify to you that they knew about the zones and the members of the KLA. Before the statement started, he pointed some wooden sticks to me and said, Do you see this? So it's the wood stick that carried -- conducted the interview, not the wish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just explain this, please, if you can. If they knew this already, why were they asking you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know why they were asking these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's see something else that you presumably claim they simply put down for you to sign: "A few days ago a KLA staff was placed in Rance village and will direct Petrastica and the other villages while," and the number of other villages including Racak are mentioned there, "will fall under the Rance village staff." Now, whoever's written that seems to know an awful lot about what the KLA are up to, don't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've heard many things about the KLA there in that office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And outside that office, I suggest, and you are telling your friends in the office exactly what you've heard. That's what you're doing here, and you're now distancing yourself from it as far as you can run from it, aren't you? That's what you're doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not distancing myself from what I've said. But I will repeat it again, that in most of the cases they would ask, Is this true? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And I would, Yes. Is there a headquarters in Rance? Yes. Is this this person here? Yes. But I'm glad that there's no name from -- persons from my village because at that time they had no idea that there were members of the KLA from our village. So I'm glad that none of the names of persons from my village is mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to go on through the rest of the document because I have no doubt you'll give us the same answers. I want to ask you this: Were you then and are you now in any way motivated by a hatred of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The truth is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you refused to have an Albanian interpreter on one of the sessions you had with the ICTY investigators? Don't you trust Albanians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not that I don't trust them, but, sir, at that time after the war people were still being killed. And I had received phone calls while I was in the western countries telling me, Be careful because people want to trace you, they want to kill you. So that's why I wanted non-Albanian speakers so that I wouldn't be identified. It was just a question of survival for me to get to here, what I am now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were with an ICTY investigator --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me, I just ask for a reference, because I think that misstates the evidence. I think it was the CCIU that he was referring to. That was my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'll be corrected. It's transcript from yesterday, page 61. Give me a moment. And it's line 16 -- Mr. Whiting is quite right. It's CCIU. "Because of the fact that the interpreter with the CCIU was a German, I refused to have an Albanian for an interpreter," in dealing with drawings he made in 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's stick with the month of August, but let's go back a little earlier than that, please. I want to ask you about another meeting you had with the Serbs briefly, and that is a meeting of the (redacted) (redacted) or thereabouts with (redacted). You remember being asked questions about this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a pure coincidence, was it, that here you are again in Mr. (redacted) office on (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You agreed with Mr. Mansfield yesterday when you said that the statement that came out of that meeting was -- or rather, the note, I'm sorry, the official note was, Mr. Mansfield's words, detailed and careful a description. That's what you told us about it yesterday. Do you remember saying that to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which notes were careful and detailed? I did not understand this quite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a good question and it is my fault. Let me put that in front of you again. You had them in front of you yesterday in Albanian, I shall do the same again. This is the second (redacted) meeting now, (redacted). Again, I remind you we're in open session so be careful about names. This is the document you described as a detailed and careful description of a number of events regarding your kidnapping and detention. Do you remember now telling us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you in this meeting before Mr. Mansfield put this note to you that you referred solely to the killings in the forest. I want to ask you a different question about this document. Bearing in mind the words "detailed" and "careful," can you tell us why Qerqiz isn't mentioned here and the wicked beatings that you received at his wicked hand time after time after time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When the worst part, the killing, took part [as interpreted], I forgot the wickedness from Qerqiz. I was no longer interested in the beatings; it was a minor thing compared to a killing. I was focused on the killing itself, and I was in a position before an authority who did not believe me that I was there in that position. They thought that I went there to fight and that I escaped. On the one hand I had the killing; on the other hand I had the authorities saying I was there to fight and abandoned the ranks just before the Serb forces took over. So it was a moment of me surviving this situation. The time difference between the killing and the thing with the authorities was very short. So this is the reason why I didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "It was a minor thing compared to a killing." True perhaps, but I wonder why you just didn't mention, Look, there's an old friend of mine, someone I know really well who's a real monster in that village. His name's Musliu; they call him Qerqizi. What was stopping you saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I answered your question, sir. I don't see a need to repeat myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you the next one then. At the bottom of the second page of that document you mention another Musliu, Musli Musliu. When you were giving them that name, did it not occur to you to say, Oh yeah, there's another Musliu I've got to tell you about. He's a monster. Do something about him, please. I suppose you would give me the same answer, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A different answer. Well, then give me the different answer if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will give you a different answer. When I mentioned Musli Musliu in that moment, I was referring to an evidence so that they believe me what had really happened. And for me to make them believe was to tell them how many persons were killed there, how many persons were in the prison. So my evidence there was not, I was beaten by Qerqiz. In that moment I was fighting for my release to leave Kosovo. When I came back to put things straight, that's when I mentioned the name of Qerqiz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fighting for your release from Kosovo, all the more reason to give these people as much information as you could. Would you not agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm telling you the truth. I told them the truth, and they did not trust me let alone to add things to it. They would not believe me. I was telling them the truth what I had seen there with my own eyes and they didn't believe me. They were saying, No, you are fighting there. How come you went there from (redacted) to a prison? You went there to fight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or is it because you hadn't got the name Qerqiz yet fed to you by (redacted) later? Isn't that the reason? His name's not there. You didn't know who this monster was then, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I knew even before that time who Isak Musliu was. (redacted) 7 (redacted), who was a KLA member and who came to the shop. (redacted) (redacted). I knew Salih whom I saw in Lapusnik. His name was Salih, his real name. I had many close persons that I knew and who were members of the KLA and who have told me things, although they were afraid to speak about what they knew. And they have told me things because they trusted me. Here I needed just a proof for the killings because I wanted to leave, because the Serbs would do something to you without any reason. They would take you and beat you up without any reason, as it happened throughout the war --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. But, Witness, what you were telling the Serbs was music to their ears. You were telling them that the KLA were behaving like animals. They'd want to know everything, wouldn't they? So why didn't you tell them about Qerqiz? The suggestion I make to you is because you hadn't been fed his name yet. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know his name. I knew the name of the other person from Mollopole, Hoxha. I had heard already the name of Celiku, of Voglushi, of Tamuli. These are names that I knew during my time in prison but that I didn't not [as interpreted] mention on this occasion. Because when they asked who carried out that killing? This and this person. So that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's move to another name, shall we? And we'll come back to what you say Qerqiz did at the end. (redacted), you've spoken about him already, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he an enemy?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have bad or good with him. I would say that it was more good things that we shared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he someone you would believe on his oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what the reason would be for this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't understand your answer. If my question was not clear, please tell me, I'll repeat it. Is he someone you would believe on his oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Depends. On what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh yes, it certainly does. Tell me something, have you ever worn a Serb police uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never. I'm positive that I have never ever wore a Serb uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason on earth why (redacted) in a signed statement to investigators of this Tribunal should say that you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This can happen because (redacted) was released from the prison. And it could be the same thing as myself, for example, when I was at the office of Jasovic, was it like this? Yes. It could have happened with him the same thing. If that is the case, then according to his words I can become Milosevic's deputy and -- let alone wear a Serb uniform. As for me, I have never worn a Serb uniform. The only uniform I wore was during my military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me tell you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the 15th of December, 1985, to 16th of December --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me tell you, this statement that I've been looking at by (redacted) wasn't taken by Dragan Jasovic, it was taken by Ole Lehtinen. You couldn't get any further from Dragan Jasovic than Ole Lehtinen, an investigator of this Tribunal. He wouldn't be pleased to hear that you were comparing him to Mr. Jasovic, no, sir. This witness said this to Lehtinen in a signed statement, and I am asking you whether it is true. He says: "I often saw him wearing a uniform used by the Serb police." Do you deny it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I categorically deny it because it never existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to your identification of Qerqiz as the man who more than once beat you. That is the topic I want to deal with next, please. Let me give you this opportunity and ask you this question: Is there any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. possibility of a mistake in your identification of Qerqiz?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I absolutely am not mistaken here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that your mind or your memory has played you false?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not about memory. I have seen the person and I cannot add anything. I've told what has happened with Qerqiz. I have stated that I haven't seen him every day, and I have stated those times that I have seen him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that you have truly convinced yourself that it was him, particularly when family members have told you that is what they believe, too? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it only here in this room two and a half days ago that you remembered for the first time that Qerqiz had a beard? Because you've never said that before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have said this before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you haven't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Qerqiz at the time when I saw him, he didn't have a long beard. He had a moustache and he had a beard resembling a person who did not shave for a week or a month. His hair was not very long and his beard, as I said, was not very long. It resembled someone who hasn't shaven for a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A month. And that's not something you've just remembered, that was always the case, was it? That memory of him, a man unshaven for at least a month or about a month was always the way he looked to you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then why didn't you tell anyone that until two days ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not asked. As I said, when I was asked, Who did you know? I would say, Qerqiz. Who did you see? Qerqiz's cousin, Salih. He was in the same room with me, with (redacted), and with (redacted) --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm not going to let you divert and I'm not going to let you get away with that answer I wasn't asked. In your witness statement to this Tribunal you give your one and only description of this man and you have him with a moustache and not a beard. Now, I'm asking you why didn't you tell them he had a beard? Or have you just remembered it? Or have you found out since he had a beard? What's the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't realised it since now because I've seen persons who have this long beard and I have seen shorter beards. And when a person has grown a beard for a week or two or a month then you don't call it a beard but you call it a person who hasn't shaved. So we usually say for someone who has a beard if the beard is this long. At that time I'm saying that it resembles someone who had not shaved for a month; it's approximate time. This is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember telling us yesterday I think -- no, when Mr. Whiting was asking you questions, forgive me, that you were shown photographs of the man you identified as Isak Musliu. Do you remember telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was in 2002.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact is you'd been shown photographs before that, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you had. On the 17th of August, 2001, by someone called Kereakes, an investigator of this Tribunal showed you photographs of Isak Musliu. So when you were identifying him in 2002, you'd already seen pictures of him, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, now I remember. He showed me the photographs with the CCIU. I have about five or six statements with the investigators. Now I remember which was the first and which was the second time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you watch the coverage of this trial when it began on TV? I'm sorry, on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some parts. There were parts that I could not follow but that I wanted to follow but that I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a bit that you could have followed. Did you hear my opening statement on behalf of Isak Musliu and see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I later -- from other sessions, I realised that you were Isak Musliu's lawyer. As for the opening statement, I don't remember whether I've seen it or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember me putting a photograph on the screen of Isak Musliu wearing a beard standing behind Fatmir Limaj? Did you see that photograph on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember seeing that photograph. I've seen many things, but not what you are mentioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody else in the world tell you they'd seen a picture from this trial of Isak Musliu with a beard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please explain it to me once again. I don't understand who you are referring to when you say, Were you told by someone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By anyone. Did anyone tell you they had seen a picture of Isak Musliu with a beard? And does that explain why two days ago you mentioned beard for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody told me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this man who you knew well could identify easily beat you and beat you and beat you and didn't bother to put a mask on his face. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see a person wearing a mask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are of course someone who is prepared to name people, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave the name of the third gunman to investigators, didn't you? Mr. Guy-Smith asked you about him this morning [sic].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which third person? During the killing or at the prison or where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, during the killing, the third executioner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previously translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you gave that statement to ICTY investigators which you did in 2002, did you stop and think for the moment about the possible consequences for that gentleman, that innocent gentleman, whose name you gave them? Did you stop and think about that or didn't you care?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've also considered -- I've always considered these facts because it's a very difficult thing to do and to say something for a person, and that person has not done that thing. As for the third person, I did not know him. I wasn't sure who he was. I thought that the CCIU will conduct an investigation and find out who this person was and whether he participated in the killing or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here is the question and answer from a statement made by you on the 2nd of August, 2002, and please bear in mind what you've just told Their Honours: "I did not know him. I wasn't sure who he was." "Q. -- Just a minute. Wait for the question. "Q. As we know, you were in the group who was not released and taken by three suspects to the mountains near Berisa. The -- there these suspects started to shoot you and kill most of your group. One of the suspects was Shala; the second was Murrizi. And from the third suspect, so far nothing was known," speaks the investigator. "Today," he says, "you've mentioned the third name of the suspect who took part in the killing. Why haven't you told the CCIU this name before?" "A. I just learned it from (redacted) about two months ago on the phone." And then you give the man's name, Nexhmedin Krashiqi from a village I won't name. It's not necessary. You didn't hesitate to stick up a name simply because (redacted) gave it to you. That's what you do to get your revenge, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why do you say the 2nd August, 2002? I don't get it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because that's the date of the interview I've just been reading from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 2nd of August, 2002, you said?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It's in front of you. It's in your right hand. You're holding it. You put up a name simply because (redacted) gave it to you; that's what you do, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't (redacted) who gave me the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, does that matter? Does that really matter? This is an innocent man you're accusing of a brutal murder. Don't you care?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the form of the question. There's nothing to establish whether this person is innocent or guilty or who knows. He's providing a name, providing information, but characterising it that way misstates the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, characterising this man as innocent doesn't misstate anything he is. The nature of the answer, I would respectfully submit, is nothing more nor less than an allegation of murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting's point is that your question went on to suggest that the man named was innocent, and he objects that there's nothing to establish guilt or innocence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are all innocent until any of us are proven guilty in a properly constituted court of law. I don't think I'm unentitled to describe this gentleman who is out there in the world and perhaps even listening as we speak as an innocent man. No court has found him otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can certainly suggest, I expect, although I don't know the facts, that he's ever been charged with this by anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: He's been interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I know nothing of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I do because I asked Mr. Whiting that precautionary question this very afternoon. If Your Honour thinks the language is too flamboyant, then I take it no further. But in my respectful submission, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think your point's been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is, sir, that you throughout have been very heavily reliant, haven't you, on information other people have given you. That's the case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The names that I have seen in the prison I relied on myself because I was an eyewitness. With exception of Qerqiz, the discovery of Shala's name and others according to information (redacted) helped me with to find the assassins. According to Qerqiz I didn't need anything to say anything about him. Prior to the war I heard from people whom he knows very well. He has worked with them, they are in KLA. They are (redacted) (redacted). As to Shala, Celik, Murrizi, I heard from (redacted) because I was interested to find out the truth. This is how it was. Because I couldn't go anywhere to ask for Shala. When I went to Kosova, I had to think twice before I went somewhere because I knew that imminent for me. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, there's just a few more questions that I have for you and I promise that I shall finish well within the allotted time this evening. And I hope, therefore, that subject to Mr. Whiting's questions of you this will be the last day of your evidence. When you gave evidence to us two days ago, you told us - and I'm looking at day 24, the uncorrected version, at page 11 of the transcript dealing with Lapusnik -- or rather, Musliu. I'm sorry. You said that in late April or beginning of May that you heard that the leader of the Rance point was Isak Musliu. First of all, do you recall telling us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that still your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is what we heard. We heard of him as being the person in charge of that point. This is what people from (redacted) or Racak said, that the point was formed and that this man was the person in charge of it. I didn't see the actual point and the actual person on the site. I heard it from people in the village and from Racak village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason I ask the question is because I suggest, and it is my client's case, that there was no point at Rance until at least the 26th of June. Are you prepared to accept that or do you disagree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot prove it. I just heard people when they came in the night. They were coming from Rance. It was end of April/early May. This is what I heard then. But in fact I didn't see the point with my own eyes. If you are asking me what people said during that time, this is what they said, even LDK activists said that, not just ordinary people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand entirely where you're getting your information from. Thank you. What I also want to suggest to you - and this may also have been the subject of gossip in the village shop and elsewhere - is that it was not until at least early August that Isak Musliu, Qerqiz, became a commander. And the commander he became commander of was the 121st Brigade, formed in August. Now, did you hear gossip to that effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything about that. I don't know what role he played in the command, but I know what he did in the prison. When he came there, Shala obeyed to his orders. When Qerqizi was not there, Murrizi was under Shala's orders. As to Qerqizi's role, what command he led, this I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us on oath two days ago that you knew Musliu, that you knew him for a long time, that you knew his family. Do you mean to tell this Court that before the war you have had conversations with Isak Musliu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We met in the street. We greeted each other. The road, it crosses to his village. It was just normal acquaintance of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest he was no such thing. I suggest you have never spoken, you have never met. But I do suggest you may well have known him and what he looked like because he was well-known in his village and in his area. Do you care to comment on that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true that I knew him. I knew him by sight, which family he came from, which village he was from. And as I said, we greeted each other like every ordinary people. This is normal in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I summarise the position in this way, I hope carefully enough for everyone's benefit: I suggest that you knew of him but you did not know him. I suggest that is the case. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with you because I knew him before the war. When I first saw him, I knew him as Qerqizi. After the war, I also know him and now I know him, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I turn now to the considerable amount of evidence you have given regarding his activities, regarding you and others, in the camp. And I can take this very shortly indeed in the light of the suggestions I made to you getting on for three hours ago. Qerqiz or Isak Musliu was not at or in that camp at any time, certainly at no time when you were there. I'm suggesting to you that you have made a terrible mistake. I hope my suggestion is clear. Do you follow it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I follow you very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
